notes.claim: Strain is a fractional change in length, so it has no units, and stress is force per area.
At low stress the deformation is in direct proportion to the stress, and the constant of proportionality is the elastic modulus (Young's modulus for tension), which is the stiffness.
Yield strength marks where plastic (permanent) deformation begins, and the 0.2% offset line is the usual practical way to find it for metals.
Tensile strength is the highest point on the stress-strain curve, a different number from the yield strength and from the modulus.
A shear load acts along the face of a cut, sliding one side past the other, as across a pin or a key; its shear stress is that force over the area of the cut (i3).
A ductile metal stretches a long way and necks before it breaks and soaks up more energy, so it is tougher; a brittle material breaks with hardly any permanent stretch (i3).
Toughness is the energy a material absorbs before it breaks, given by the area under its stress-strain curve (i3).
Hardness is how well a material resists denting or scratching, a different property from stiffness and strength (i3).
